2610.12617v1.title: GeopoliticalQA: Benchmarking Retrieval and Generation over Intelligence Reports
2610.12617v1.authors: Veronika Solopova, Ivan Havlytskyi, Viktoria Skorik, Ostap Vykhopen
2610.12617v1.ori_summary: Geopolitical and strategic intelligence reports constitute a rich source of expert knowledge and have increasing value in the current political climate, but their heterogeneity and analytical complexity pose challenges for retrieval-augmented question answering. We introduce a benchmark for grounded question answering over 415 open-source geopolitical and strategic intelligence reports, comprising 5,525 document-grounded question-answer pairs spanning factual, inferential, comparative, and risk-oriented questions. We propose a document-aware generation pipeline that profiles reports before generating questions and validate dataset quality through expert annotation and an LLM-as-judge protocol. Using the benchmark, we evaluate 15 retrieval systems and six open-weight LLMs for RAG. We find that models perform similarly on document-level retrieval, while at the harder chunk level retrieval quality is not driven by embedding-model scale: bge-m3, a mid-size open encoder matches an order of magnitude larger ones and outperforms commercial embedding APIs. In contrast, answer generation remains challenging even given the gold evidence, particularly for inferential and risk-oriented questions.
2610.12617v1.reasoning: A geopolitical QA benchmark unrelated to ranking, recommendation, or auction mechanisms.

2610.13810v1.title: Tracing and Taming Hallucinated Terms via Subsequence-Association Filtering and Breadth-Aware Selection for LLM Query Expansion
2610.13810v1.authors: Amit Kumar Jaiswal, Sagar Uprety, Prayag Tiwari
2610.13810v1.ori_summary: Large language models (LLMs) are now a standard source of query expansion terms but they hallucinate. They inject non existent entities and off-topic terms that add ranking noise and can hurt strong retrievers. Existing remedies such as corpus grounding, mutual verification and preference alignment treat hallucinated terms as an undifferentiated nuisance to be filtered by agreement heuristics, without a mechanistic account of why a given term appears or a principled criterion for how many terms to keep. We propose Subsequence-Association Filtered, breadth-aware query expansion (SAFE-QE), a training-free, retriever agnostic method that draws on the subsequence-association account of hallucination. We score each candidate expansion term by its corpus conditioned cross-context reproducibility, terms that reappear under randomised query contexts yet lack support in the pseudo-relevant set are flagged as products of dominant hallucinatory associations and down-weighted. Drawing on the characterisation of language generation as a trade-off between consistency (no hallucination) and breadth (coverage), we cast term selection as constrained coverage maximisation over the pseudo-relevant set, keeping a set that is approximately broad but consistent and stable across resampling. We also introduce the Hallucinated Expansion Term Rate, a query side faithfulness metric that counts injected expansion terms no relevant document supports. We evaluate our approach on benchmarked TREC and BEIR collections. Our SAFE-QE is statistically indistinguishable from generative and corpus-steered expansion on nDCG@10 while injecting fewer unsupported terms 4.3 per query against 27.8 for Query2doc and 57.5 for HyDE and on a strong learned sparse retriever, where every expansion method regresses. Faithfulness is therefore available at no measurable cost in ranking quality.
2610.13810v1.reasoning: LLM hallucination mitigation in query expansion, not ranking or mechanism design.

2610.13128v1.title: Locate, Judge, Read: Role-Specialized Tool Agents over a Knowledge-Point Index for Open-Domain Multimodal Document QA
2610.13128v1.ori_summary: Question answering over large heterogeneous document collections requires first finding the right passages and then reading them, yet current retrieval-augmented agents give one model both kinds of tools and let it schedule itself. We present KnowForge, a pipeline separated by job: a hybrid-retrieval knowledge-point index; a Locator agent that can only search; a code-scheduled bridge judge that forces the missing second hop; a typed, size-bounded evidence pool that merges every search's ranking; a Deep Reader agent that can only read text, images and tables; and a synthesizer with a format checker. With a self-hosted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (3B active), KnowForge reaches F1 47.5 on the full open-domain M3DocVQA (2,441 questions, 3,368 PDFs), +11.0 over the published M3DocRAG system and +7.1 over one-shot retrieve-and-answer on the same index and model, and 53.5 with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. On MultiHop-RAG it reaches 73.5 accuracy, above the strongest published RAG and GraphRAG results (71.2); on the single-document MMLongBench-Doc it lifts the same model from 34.8 to 47.0, level with GPT-4o reading page images (46.3). Per-job ablations on the full benchmarks attribute the gain: the Deep Reader is worth 3.8, 9.8 and 0 points on the three corpora, tracking how visual each is; merging both agents into one with all tools and twice the rounds loses 1.9 F1 because it keeps searching instead of reading; a round-budget sweep shows a step at four Locator rounds and a plateau beyond; query latency scales with model calls rather than corpus size. We serve the three indexed benchmarks as read-only knowledge bases (free registration) and release all prompts and the runner code: https://github.com/metask-ai/knowforge-bench

2610.13648v1.title: SPARQL-LLM in the TEXT2SPARQL 2026 Challenge
2610.13648v1.authors: Panayiotis Smeros, Vincent Emonet, Ruijie Wang, Ana-Claudia Sima, Tarcisio Mendes de Farias

2610.13948v1.title: Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?
2610.13948v1.authors: Alexander Hickey, Joanna Knight, James Bishop
2610.13948v1.ori_summary: Language models increasingly support or automate information retrieval from document collections too large to index. This task is difficult when it requires specialist linguistic or scientific knowledge. We used the Wikipedia Game to test language models on an analogous information retrieval task. In the game, players must reach a target article using only article links. We compared sentence embedding models and LLMs across five Wikipedia languages and five academic-literature datasets. We construct very large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and of paper citations using OpenAlex and provide code to build and navigate them. This allows the study of language models' navigation capabilities without relying on third-party APIs. We compared the models with human and TF-IDF benchmarks. The Wikipedia Game format enables robust comparisons across techniques, languages, and domains. No model significantly outperformed humans, although the best models (GPT-o3 mini, GPT-4o, QwQ:32B, and DeepSeek-R1:70B) achieved comparable success. Performance and rankings varied across languages and topics, with implications for practitioners utilising these techniques.

2610.13416v1.title: Web$hell: A Unified Interface for Agentic Web Access
2610.13416v1.authors: Sunghwan Kim, Deogyong Kim, Sangam Lee, Donguk Kwon, Dongha Lee
2610.13416v1.ori_summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming direct users of the open web. As they take on increasingly complex and information-intensive tasks, effective web access is becoming a core capability for agentic problem solving. Existing approaches have advanced agentic web access through different access models, including search-augmented agents, browser-based agents, and, more recently, filesystem-based agents. Nevertheless, as users expect agents to complete long-horizon, end-to-end tasks, they increasingly need to conduct broad information gathering, perform browser actions, and revisit acquired evidence within a single trajectory. Yet our preliminary analyses reveal that existing access models struggle to meet these demands. They primarily support either information gathering or browser interaction, while combining their capabilities can involve substantial costs or performance trade-offs. To this end, we present Web\$hell, an interface that unifies web access under a single access model. Using a common schema defined by WebContract, WebCompiler compiles live webpages into addressable information and action objects. These objects are maintained in WebCache and handled through a shared set of operations, providing agents with consistent, operable, and persistent web access. Through extensive experiments across web search, web navigation, and deep research benchmarks, we show that Web\$hell achieves strong task performance at lower cost. Our results further indicate the importance of interface design for effective web access, with Web\$hell opening new possibilities for more capable and efficient LLM agents on the web.
2610.13416v1.reasoning: Agentic web access interface, not ranking or auction mechanism related.

2610.13314v1.title: NEAR: Neighborhood-Aware Residuals for Memory Retrieval
2610.13314v1.authors: Han Luo, Zhan Zhuang, Xu He, Jujia Zhao, Yu Li, Suqin Yuan, Dong Li, Lei Feng
2610.13314v1.ori_summary: Memory retrieval aims to identify evidence from stored records to answer a query. Stored records with different factual details may share topics, entities, or events. Such shared contents would make records without the required evidence more likely to receive high similarity scores and outrank the correct evidence. In this paper, we use the information shared by these records to construct local references for query-memory matching. We propose NEighborhood-Aware Residuals (NEAR), a training-free framework that uses these references to construct residual representations that complement the original embeddings. Specifically, each memory derives a reference direction from its neighbors, and each query obtains its reference from a precomputed table. Using these references, NEAR constructs projection residuals for both queries and memories. These residuals are combined with the original embeddings for a single approximate nearest-neighbor search over a fixed memory index. Experiments on eight long-context retrieval benchmarks show consistent improvements across nine embedding models. Downstream evaluations show that NEAR improves question-answering performance.

2610.13296v1.title: PRIME: Pre-Retrieval Index Modeling Enhancement for Structured Document Retrieval-Real
2610.13296v1.ori_summary: High-precision retrieval over external knowledge bases is essential for LLM agents to operate effectively. However, existing Information Retrieval (IR) research primarily optimizes query-side retrievers (e.g., ColBERT, BGE) and generators (e.g., Self-RAG, GraphRAG), while reducing corpus-side representation to chunking. This leaves index-side quality an underexplored lever. We propose Pre-Retrieval Index Modeling & Enhancement (PRIME), an index-side optimization framework built on two complementary tracks: an LLM-driven Semantic Restructuring (SR) track that transforms long documents into structured, information-dense sections, and a deterministic Metadata Synthesis (MS) and Hierarchical Retrieval (HR) track that extracts semantic anchors and heading structure for coarse-to-fine section retrieval. Our evaluations show that deterministic metadata matches structure-aware chunking's retrieval quality while cutting embedding computation by 45.8 $\times$ and index vector count by 22.4 $\times$. On top of these gains, Semantic Restructuring (SR) further improves Answer-F1 by 13.7% in full deployment, with characterized quality-fidelity-cost trade-offs. Across QASPER, BRIGHT, and NFCorpus, we further characterize three qualitative regimes that determine whether index-side optimization helps or degrades retrieval, while showing that these index-side effects are neutralized under a strong reranker.

2610.13277v1.title: Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence
2610.13277v1.authors: Han Luo, Zhan Zhuang, Xu He, Jujia Zhao, Yu Li, Suqin Yuan, Dong Li, Lei Feng
2610.13277v1.ori_summary: Memory-augmented assistants retrieve evidence from stored conversations and documents to answer queries. Such local evidence can be matched to queries using the contextual token representations already computed by the same embedding models. Our method uses sparse token matching to improve retrieval without additional training. Each query token retrieves a small set of matching tokens across candidate memories. The matching scores are aggregated for each memory and combined with whole-memory similarity to rank memories. An optional low-rank query adapter can be trained with supervision while keeping the encoder and stored memory representations fixed. Our method improves retrieval across eight benchmarks and multiple model families without additional training. Query adaptation further increases the gains to 13.3 and 14.3 percentage points in average Recall@10 and NDCG@10 on Qwen3-Embedding-4B. These retrieval gains translate into higher question-answering accuracy on long-term memory benchmarks.

2610.13889v1.title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics
2610.13889v1.ori_summary: As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED (Reliability-Aware Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent, a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query-tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Elliotes/EcoAgent.

2610.13504v1.title: Beyond Temporal Proximity: Explanatory World Models for Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning
2610.13504v1.authors: Oriol Corcoll, Qiyao Wei, Ciarán Mark Gilligan-Lee
2610.13504v1.ori_summary: Generative Recommenders increasingly use Reinforcement Learning (RL) to optimize outcomes that may appear hundreds or thousands of interactions after a decision. Standard RL propagates reward according to temporal proximity rather than explicit relevance, attenuating the signal assigned to distant but important actions and creating a source of sample inefficiency. We introduce Explanatory World Models (EWM), an attribution framework that uses explanations to identify the earlier events that plausibly contributed to a realized outcome. We instantiate EWM with a frontier language model and use its explanations as learning signals using a conservative hierarchical operator that recursively redistributes reward while preserving the undiscounted episode return. To investigate what constitutes a useful explanation, we operationalize three complementary variants inspired by Halpern's actual causation, Lombrozo's explanatory simplicity, and Deutsch's hard-to-vary explanations. We evaluate EWM on two controlled long-horizon RL benchmarks, a public sequential-recommendation benchmark, and an industry-scale generative recommender. On Crafter and WordCraft, EWM substantially outperforms PPO and LaRe, with its largest gains when rewards are most delayed. On KuaiRand, EWM outperforms SFT and LaRe offline and A2C online. Finally, in an offline evaluation of an industry generative recommender, EWM considerably improves Recall and increases behavioral proxies. These results suggest that explanations can provide structured and reusable credit for learning from delayed outcomes.
2610.13504v1.reasoning: Pure RL credit assignment paper with no ranking, re-ranking, or auction mechanism application.

2610.12757v1.title: MADS: Multi-Agent Dialog Simulation for Robust Conversational Agents
2610.12757v1.authors: Arkajyoti Chakraborty, Adam Zernik, Ishika Kulkarni, Mudit Arora, Hugo Lin, Justin Chiu, Alessandro Di Bari, Neha Gupta, Andreas Stolcke
2610.12757v1.ori_summary: Task-oriented conversational agents remain fragile under realistic conditions, especially when users exhibit non-cooperative behavior. 2610.12707v1.title: Unsupervised Multimodal Reward Modeling
2610.12707v1.authors: Yueying Li, Jingxuan Fan, Kianté Brantley, Sham M. Kakade, Hanlin Zhang
2610.12707v1.ori_summary: Vision-language reward models are trained on annotated preference pairs, which are expensive to collect, can disagree, and are ranked by benchmark accuracy. The layer is the decisive choice, worth 5.8 points over the last layer, and one recipe transferred without re-tuning beats or at least matches GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B, 6.6 points ahead on VL-RewardBench, from a few thousand parameters at about a thousandth of fine-tuning compute. At an equal pair budget, perturbations teach a frozen head 3 to 5 points more than curated RLAIF-V pairs. Because the backbone is frozen, the objective is convex, and the perturbation sampler specifies the reward, which the benchmark does not identify: two heads trained on disjoint halves of the same perturbations tie on the benchmark and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging. 2610.12669v1.title: GeoFitBench-LLM: A Benchmark for Assessing Large Language Models' Capabilities in Geospatial Data Requirements Elicitation for Geo-Analytic Tasks
2610.12669v1.authors: Amirhossein Vahdat, Thierry Badard, Luc Lamontagne

2610.12667v1.title: perturber: A Stateless Service for Semantics-Preserving Text Perturbations
2610.12667v1.ori_summary: Large language model (LLM) evaluations on clean benchmarks overstate model robustness: real inputs arrive perturbed, and these meaning-preserving variants routinely move model answers. Studying this systematically requires applying perturbations one at a time, reproducibly, and identically wherever they run, yet existing tools couple them to a benchmarking stack rather than packaging them as a reusable transform layer. We present perturber, a stateless service and Python library that applies exactly one semantics-preserving perturbation per call, drawn from a first-party catalog of 68 perturbations across 11 families. It turns on a single primitive, with composition left to the caller chaining calls, so the service and the library produce identical output by construction. We evaluate the tool itself, its correctness, reproducibility, and cost, rather than any model's robustness, measuring meaning-preservation per perturbation rather than assuming it. The demonstration adds a live playground, an introspectable catalog for benchmark selection, and a one-command reproducible evaluation.

2610.12602v1.title: Self-Preservation in Language Models
2610.12602v1.authors: Dongkyu Cho, Rumi Chunara, Ali Behrouz
2610.12602v1.ori_summary: Continual learning (CL) seeks to adapt pretrained models while preserving prior capabilities. Yet the tasks supplied for preservation cover only part of what a model knows, while forgetting can extend beyond them. Recent work shows that language models can supplement this limited evidence by generating useful replay without access to their original training data. This raises a question about self-preservation: can a model help choose preservation targets that protect its own capabilities more broadly? Continual instruction tuning with Qwen models of varying sizes yields three findings. First, the new task and learning rate shape which prior capabilities degrade, while tracking previously correct answers reveals losses that average accuracy can conceal. Second, generated replay reduces forgetting on tasks outside the bank. Combining partial banks strengthens this protection, improving mean retention of previously correct answers over either bank alone across the tested sizes. Third, the model can also help choose replay targets: selection informed by the new task improves mean held-out retention over random selection at 4B, with similar new-task gains, although smaller models show no corresponding advantage. Under a fixed example budget, however, replacing new-task examples with replay improves preservation at the cost of smaller new-task gains. Together, these findings show that models can support broader self-preservation by generating replay data and, in some settings, choosing which tasks to replay.
2610.12602v1.reasoning: Studies language model self-preservation behavior; unrelated to ranking models or auction mechanisms.

2610.13059v1.title: CliQ-RRG: Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation
2610.13059v1.authors: Chandravardhan Singh Raghaw, Shahid Shafi Dar, Arnav Nishith Sharma, Shrey Modi, Nagendra Kumar

2610.13025v1.title: Evo$^2$: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution
2610.13025v1.authors: Chejian Xu, Shujian Zhang, Wenxuan Zhou, John Lambert, Beck Chen, Bo Li, Andrew Hard, Rajiv Mathews
2610.13025v1.ori_summary: Self-evolving agents are increasingly used to improve language model systems without human intervention through either weight updates or harness improvements. Existing approaches typically pursue these directions separately: some methods update model weights using self-generated experience, while others rewrite the harness that defines how an agent uses prompts, tools, context, and execution feedback. However, these approaches overlook the relationship between model weights and the agent harness. To connect these processes and ensure effective and smooth agent self-evolving, we propose Evo$^2$, a framework for weight-harness co-evolution. For harness updates, we design a unified dual-role pipeline that a single policy serves as both a Proposer, which writes harness edits, and a Reflector, which diagnoses their effects and guides revision. For weight updates, harness modifications and their execution outcomes guide the training of both the Proposer and the Reflector. We further develop EvoTIDE, a training pipeline that recovers usable trajectories through edit extraction and prefix continuation, then combines SFT with interleaved GRPO across the two roles. Extensive experiments across three coding benchmarks demonstrate that Evo$^2$ significantly outperforms existing self-evolution methods. It achieves 82.1% on Polyglot and 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified, compared with 62.6% and 41.0% for the strongest baseline, respectively. We also show that the evolved harnesses transfer to different tasks without further evolution and rank first in cross-benchmark evaluations. Our dual-role harness improvement framework is also able to extend to self-evolution with proprietary models, improving a GPT-5-mini agent's performance from 24.4% to 48.3%. These results demonstrate the applicability of the framework Evo$^2$ across domains and its broad transferability across models and tasks.

2610.12841v1.title: Fear Is Not Always Fear: Variation in Emotion Label Equivalence Across Datasets
2610.12841v1.ori_summary: Emotion classifiers are routinely applied beyond their training data, on the assumption that same-named labels such as fear or surprise mean the same thing across resources. We test this assumption for five labels shared by GoEmotions, XED, and BRIGHTER, comparing models on identical inputs and under cross-corpus transfer. On the same texts, one fear classifier flags 71% as fearful and another 8%, yet the two largely agree on how the texts rank. Across 30 resource-label comparisons, training-label prevalence explains about half of this kind of scale mismatch, and a fitted intercept removes most of it. What recalibration cannot repair is larger: transferred models lose 55% of native discrimination in aggregate, agreement in ranking between classifiers is only weakly related to that loss, and for surprise the resources disagree about which texts express the emotion. The choice of training resource can therefore change conclusions: on two external tweet collections, BRIGHTER- and XED-trained classifiers give opposite answers about which shows more surprise, even after rank normalization, with intervals excluding zero in both directions. A shared emotion label name does not establish an interchangeable measurement target.

2610.12837v1.title: COFFEQA: Counterfactual-Guided Few-Shot Distillation for LLM Question Answering
2610.12837v1.ori_summary: Knowledge distillation aims to train a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model for resource-constrained environments. However, the process of distillation is typically data-intensive and computationally expensive, particularly for generative tasks. Few-shot distillation offers an alternative by transferring teacher knowledge using limited training samples. However, we observe that few-shot distillation performance is heavily dependent on the choice of these training samples. In fact, we demonstrate that using more uncertain samples near the teacher's decision boundary can significantly deteriorate distillation performance. Motivated by this observation, we propose Counterfactual-guided Few-shot Distillation in Open-book Question Answering (COFFEQA), a novel strategy that aptly uses counterfactuals to provide additional supervision around challenging factual samples. In the generative QA setting, we define a counterfactual as a minimally modified context that induces the teacher to change its response to an alternative answer. We provide geometric insights on how factual-counterfactual pairs can constrain the deviation between the teacher's and student's decision boundaries. 2610.12995v1.title: What Should SFT Learn? Conditional Information Gain for Generalizable Post-Training
2610.12995v1.authors: Yuxuan Gu, Kequan Niu, Xiaocheng Feng, Yun Li, Yiqiao Yang, Bing Qin

Under teacher forcing, we compare the token likelihood from a frozen reference model with and without access to the task input while keeping the gold solution prefix fixed. The resulting conditional information gain quantifies how much the task itself reduces uncertainty about the demonstrated decision. We then convert this information into a KL-regularized projection of the current policy and derive an equivalent scalar-weighted SFT objective whose logit gradient exactly matches that of the projected target. 2610.13171v1.title: PreSTO: Predictive Subtree Prefetching for Fast LLM Power Sampling
2610.13171v1.authors: Nan Jiang, Panagiotis Theodoropoulos, Wei Deng
2610.13171v1.ori_summary: Power sampling improves large language model (LLM) reasoning at test time by sampling from a sharpened version of the base model's distribution. Its sampler, PowerMH, is slow because its Metropolis--Hastings (MH) updates are sequential: each accept/reject decision sets the state from which the next proposal is generated. We also observe that MH reaches only a sparse, nearly unary part of each prefetched subtree, we further design a \textit{predictive traversal rule} that chooses the subtree to maximize the predicted number of completed transitions. Across seven datasets and five base LLMs, PreSTO achieves median speedups of $1.71\times$, $1.91\times$, and $2.33\times$ on PowerMH and its follow-ups EntropyCut and MultiTryMH, respectively; on the first two, it makes a median of $3.9\times$ fewer model calls, each only $2.1\times$ longer. 2610.13157v1.title: SOAR: Source-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Precise Credit Assignment for Search Agents
2610.13157v1.authors: Shengze Huang, Zihao Tang, Jinluan Yang, Xin Yu, Zhenghao Lin, Xiao Liu, Zengxuan Wen, Yeyun Gong, Haizhen Huang, Weiwei Deng, Feng Sun, Qi Zhang, Fei Wu, Kun Kuang

2610.13057v1.title: CoBe: A Benchmark For Conversational Counterfactual Text Editing
2610.13057v1.authors: Arvind Raghavan, Inwoo Hwang, Shreyas Havaldar, Kai-Zhan Lee, Aurghya Maiti, Yushu Pan, Jeffrey Wu, Mingxuan Li, Elias Bareinboim

2610.12601v1.title: Reflective Prompt Optimization of a Deep-Research Agent: A Topic-Disjoint, Multi-Seed Protocol for Measuring Transferable Gains and Prompt-Level Overfitting
2610.12601v1.authors: Elias Lumer, Sahil Sen, Vamse Kumar Subbiah, Kevin Paul
2610.12601v1.ori_summary: Prompt optimization is an attractive alternative to reinforcement learning for adapting language-model agents, since it is cheap and produces human-readable artifacts. 2610.12898v1.title: Rethinking the Roles of Diffusion and Decoding: Predictive-State Flows for Parallel Language Generation
2610.12898v1.authors: Jinjin He, Xinsong Feng, Lucheng Fu, Sinan Wang, Bo Zhu, Jiayun Wang
2610.12898v1.ori_summary: In continuous diffusion language models (DLMs), latents generated by the diffusion prior are mapped almost deterministically to tokens, either by a decoder or through a token embedding matrix. A rectified-flow prior generates the sequence of predictive states, after which a block-causal decoder generates all blocks in parallel, autoregressively only within each block. This design reduces diffusion from L token-level states to K << L predictive states and reduces token-level sequential depth to L/K. On unconditional OpenWebText generation, a 197M-parameter model with K=8 achieves a generative perplexity of 22.8 at entropy 5.16 using 0.31 TFLOPs per 1024-token document, versus 24.0 and 7.2 TFLOPs for ELF-B with 32 sampling steps. 2610.12939v1.title: Surfing the Activation Wave: Analyzing the Information and Geometry of LLM Hidden States for Speculative Decoding
2610.12939v1.authors: Raghavv Goel, Sudhanshu Agrawal, Mukul Gagrani, Risheek Garrepalli, Mingu Lee
2610.12939v1.ori_summary: Decoder hidden states from different layers of large language models (LLMs) often encode complementary information. As part of this framework, we introduce token-entropy filtering, which removes hidden states associated with low predictive-entropy tokens, thereby improving the quality of layer-selection statistics. 2610.12758v1.title: DistressBench: Evaluating Multi-Dimensional Crisis Support in Large Language Models
2610.12758v1.authors: Drew Rein, Patrick Oathout, Vishal Kumar, Udari Madhushani Sehwag

2610.12701v1.title: Activating the Annotator: Operationalising Lived Experience in Data Annotation
2610.12701v1.authors: Sheza Munir, Ramaravind Kommiya Mothilal, Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed

2610.13166v1.title: Scaling Agentic Data for Long-Horizon Terminal Intelligence
2610.13166v1.authors: Shun Zou, Ziyu Ma, Yi Zou, Yong Wang, Lin Chen, Zehui Chen, Guanhua Chen, Xiangxiang Chu, Feng Zhao
2610.13166v1.ori_summary: Terminal agents are moving beyond local operations toward completing real-world professional tasks. 2610.13041v1.title: RAMP: Recurrent Adaptive Mixed Precision for Efficient Prefill in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
2610.13041v1.ori_summary: Recurrent-depth language models improve inference-time reasoning by repeatedly applying a shared network to refine internal representations, but the additional recurrent computation also increases inference cost. This overhead is particularly pronounced during long-context prefill, where the full input sequence is repeatedly processed across recurrent depth. 2610.12570v1.title: Contextual Correction of Parallel Draftsfor Speculative Decoding

2610.12582v1.title: One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models

2610.12569v1.title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents
2610.12569v1.authors: Wei Minn, Zhensu Sun, Lwin Khin Shar, David Lo
2610.12569v1.ori_summary: Static coding benchmarks are fixed at release. Over time their tasks leak into training data, and stronger agents eventually saturate them. 2610.12932v1.title: SEEDS: Preview-Guided Evidence Admission for Search Agents
2610.12932v1.authors: Jiajin Liu, Chenxi Xu, Dongzhe Fan, Yuanfu Sun, Qiaoyu Tan
2610.12932v1.ori_summary: Search agents extend large reasoning models with multi-round access to external knowledge, yet most existing systems largely conflate retrieving evidence with consuming it. 2610.13605v1.title: zip2zip++: Towards Inference-Time Token Compression with Minimal Quality Loss

2610.13021v1.authors: Jie Huang, Yanan Chen, Ruixun Liu, Kaichen He, Xinyi He, Rui Huang, Zilong Zheng, Zhenliang Zhang, Yiwu Zhong
2610.13021v1.ori_summary: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. 2610.13285v1.title: BoundaryEvo: Data-Model Co-Evolution at the Capability Boundary for Long-Chain Reasoning Distillation
2610.13285v1.authors: Jiaming Su, Suorong Yang, Xudong Li, Tengchao Yang, Peng Ye

This mismatch becomes especially costly when only a small number of teacher trajectories can be used for training. Besides, examples already mastered provide little new supervision, while examples far beyond the capability of student may be difficult to learn from. Training data should therefore adapt as model capability evolves, yet reliable data selection is difficult when the student is initially weak. In Capability Priming, we directly distill a small set of teacher-generated long reasoning trajectories without using a separate model to judge and filter them, allowing the student to acquire an initial reasoning capability before capability-aware data selection. In Capability-Boundary Co-Evolution, we repeatedly select questions that the current student has not mastered but the expert can reliably solve, and update the training data as the student evolves. 2610.13337v1.title: Exploring Attention Sinks in Text-to-Image Transformers from Diffusion and Autoregressive Models
2610.13337v1.authors: Binglei Li, Mengping Yang, Zhiyu Tan, Wenxu Qian, Junping Zhang, Hao Li
2610.13337v1.ori_summary: Attention sinks are tokens or positions that consistently receive disproportionate attention mass, often beyond what their semantic content would suggest. Through systematic attention analysis and targeted interventions, we identify that attention sinks emerge in both bidirectional diffusion and autoregressive models but exhibit distinct patterns. The autoregressive model concentrates attention on the first and global-scale tokens, whereas the bidirectional models develop sinks near modality boundaries, within text regions, and at spatial corners. Moreover, these patterns vary across generation stages and are localized to a sparse subset of layers and heads. To assess their functional relevance, we perturb sink-related heads and token positions. It turns out that perturbing sink-ranked heads produces larger average changes than non-sink comparisons, while some sink-position perturbations have limited effects on bidirectional model scores. We further introduce register tokens to redistribute attention sinks and find that several configurations preserve or modestly improve generation performance. Overall, attention sinks are architecture-, inference-stage-, and component-dependent phenomena, providing a basis for mechanistic analysis and principled attention design in text-to-image transformers.

2610.13247v1.title: What Do Audio-Language Judges of Generated Music Listen For? Four Probes with Controls from Expert Ratings
2610.13247v1.ori_summary: Open audio-language models are used as judges of generated music: given a clip and its text prompt, the model rates the clip, and the judge is validated by how well its ratings correlate with expert ratings. With audio, every judge follows the clip it hears when rating prompt alignment, two do when rating musical quality, and the strongest judge's quality score tracks the experts' alignment rating more than their quality rating. The pairwise verdicts of the four smaller judges follow the position of a clip in the pair (its slot) rather than its quality on both rating sets. For musical quality, rewording the instruction moves the correlation of most judges as much as changing the judge. MusicEval's prompt assignment bounds any prompt-only judge at the model level. 2610.13194v1.title: JANUS: Enhancing Long-Horizon Autonomous Research with Co-Evolving World Models
2610.13194v1.authors: Mengdi Liu, Chenghao Jia, Hong Chang, Mingjie He, Shiguang Shan, Xilin Chen

2610.13058v1.title: Travel Back To Move Forward: Retrospective Exploration and Evolving for Long Horizon Agents
2610.13058v1.authors: Ziang Ye, Wentao Shi, Lei Chen, Zhengzhou Cai, Yu Wang, Zhiyuan Yao, Zihan Wang, Xierui Song, Fuli Feng, Yixin Cao

2610.12961v1.authors: Yingjie Zhu, Han Cheng, Xuefeng Bai, Youcheng Pan, Yang Xiang, Kehai Chen

2610.12794v1.title: Meta-Reflective Evolution Effectively Improves Production AI Systems
2610.12794v1.authors: Seung Won Wilson Yoo, Chang Zeng, Aditi Somayajula, Sahithi Ankireddy, Rohan Kosalge, Avishree Khare, John Mitchell, Aditya G. Parameswaran, Rajhans Samdani, Anupam Datta

2610.13024v1.title: What Visual Representations Do World Action Models Need?
2610.13024v1.authors: Kai Liu, Jiangran Lyu, Tingyu Deng, Yixin Zheng, Jingtian Wan, Wenbo Cui, Mi Yan, Yizhou Zhou, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang

2610.12981v1.title: The Evidence Anchoring Boundary: Where Visual Interventions Matter and When They Help in Multimodal LLMs
2610.12981v1.authors: Qiji Zhou, Junyi Hu, Peiyu Wang, Yue Zhang

2610.12978v1.title: Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers

2610.12783v1.title: Shift-Aware Identity-Guided Latent Refinement for Referring Audio--Visual Segmentation

2610.12811v1.title: Spend Where It Matters: Particle Search with MH Refinement for Budget-Constrained Audio-Visual Alignment

2610.13725v1.title: The Distortion of Threshold Approval Multiwinner Voting
2610.13725v1.authors: Mohamad Latifian, Marzieh Nilipour, Alexandros A. Voudouris
2610.13725v1.ori_summary: We study multiwinner voting with $n$ voters and $m$ candidates, where the goal is to select a committee of size $k$. Voters have unit-sum cardinal utilities but report only coarse information induced by $t$ utility thresholds. In particular, each voter partitions the candidates into approval sets, with the utilities of all candidates in the same set lying between the same pair of consecutive thresholds. We model the utility of each voter for a committee as a normalized monotone symmetric norm, capturing, among others, additive welfare, best-representative utility, top-$r$ welfare, $\ell_p$ welfare, and normalized non-increasing ordered weighted averages. We design a deterministic rule with distortion at most $2(2m)^{1/t}$ and a randomized rule with distortion at most $2\min\{m^{1/(t+1)},m/k\}$. These guarantees hold for every committee size $k$ and every norm in our framework. Consequently, a single threshold yields distortion $O(m)$ for deterministic rules and $O(\sqrt{m})$ for randomized rules, while $O(\log m)$ thresholds suffice for constant distortion. We complement these results with norm-dependent lower bounds that asymptotically match our upper bounds for constant committee sizes, including the single-winner case.
2610.13725v1.reasoning: Social choice theory on multiwinner voting, unrelated to ranking algorithms or e-commerce mechanisms.

2610.12858v1.title: The False Allure of "Security by Obscurity": A Game-Theoretic Approach
2610.12858v1.ori_summary: "Security by obscurity," or the idea that hiding how a system works helps protect it from adversaries, has long been poorly regarded in the security community. Yet its intuitive appeal persists, and it has resurfaced repeatedly in industry practices and public debates over the years. The logic, on the one hand, is that open scrutiny of systems is the best way to find and respond to problems; and on the other hand, that too much openness can increase risk by giving adversaries a roadmap for attack. This isn't purely a technical question, but a human one: it's about how attackers and good-faith security researchers respond to openness in the real world. As such, security experts base their stance on decades of community experience; however, the field lacks empirical or theoretical foundations to back up these long-standing beliefs. We provide the first rigorous modeling of "security by obscurity," aiming to capture how rational actors will respond to openness or obscurity in fallible systems. We prove that in equilibrium under realistic model conditions, "obscured" systems are more likely to suffer successful attacks than "open" systems --- establishing theoretical support for the longstanding received wisdom.
2610.12858v1.reasoning: This is a security game theory paper unrelated to ranking mechanisms.

2610.13759v1.title: Asymmetric Information in Dynamic Lending Games
2610.13759v1.authors: Kristijan Atanasov, Frederik Mallmann-Trenn, Carmine Ventre
2610.13759v1.ori_summary: We study a dynamic lending game with limited but reusable supply. Borrower arrivals and loan durations are stochastic. Demand is allocated cheapest-first, subject to available supply, so a lender's quote affects both its current payoff and its ability to serve future borrowers. Motivated by industry practice, we study this problem through the lens of information disclosure: Lenders observe either only their own available supply or also their rivals' aggregate available supply. We ask how providing this information to all, some or none of the lenders affects payoffs as demand varies relative to supply, and how these effects change when a fixed total supply is divided among different numbers of lenders. Interestingly, in the case of asymmetric information disclosure, total payoffs can increase, while total lending remains the same. We identify sufficient mathematical regimes in which this phenomenon occurs. Who receives supply information matters differently as demand rises. For the case of two lenders, informing only the larger lender yields higher total lender payoff at lower demand, while informing only the smaller lender can yield the highest total lender payoff at higher demand. For a platform deciding which lenders can observe rival supply, the results suggest that disclosure can change the fees paid by borrowers without changing how much is lent. Wider access to supply information need not lower those fees: its effect depends on who receives the information and the balance between demand and supply.
2610.13759v1.reasoning: Purely theoretical lending game study, unrelated to ranking or auction mechanisms.
